captions.instagram:
How does an air fryer work?

An air fryer never fries. It is a tiny, ferocious fan oven. Take one apart in 3D, race a potato cube in fast and still air, watch a chip's surface sit at 100 °C until it dries and browns, and see why a crowded basket cooks unevenly.

→ An air fryer is a tiny convection oven: a heater, a fan and a basket with holes in it.
→ The fan pulls air up through the glowing element and blasts it down the sides and back up through the food.
→ Moving air hands over heat far faster than still air: a fan can triple h in q = h × A × ΔT.
→ A wet chip’s surface is stuck near 100 °C until its water boils away.
→ Once it is dry, it climbs past 140 °C and the Maillard reaction browns it.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/airfryerclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does an air fryer work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
An air fryer never fries. It is a tiny, ferocious fan oven. Take one apart in 3D, race a potato cube in fast and still air, watch a chip's surface sit at 100 °C until it dries and browns, and see why a crowded basket cooks unevenly.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/airfryerclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/airfryerclear

In this video:
• A heater, a fan and a basket. An air fryer is a small convection oven.
• Moving air hands over heat fast. Heat flows into food as q = h × A × ΔT.
• Dry first, then brown. A wet surface is stuck near 100 °C, because boiling water soaks up 2,257 kJ per kilogram.
• Oil versus air. Deep-fat frying uses oil, which hands over heat far better (h about 250 to 500 W/m²K) but soaks into chips, leaving them about 10 to 15% fat.
• Let the air through. The fan throws air down the sides of the pan; a star-shaped baffle turns it up through the basket and the food.
• Click on, click off. A thermostat, a bimetal disc or an NTC sensor with a relay, switches the element fully on and off around the set point.
